reason: Quotes state IAM stores up to five versions of customer managed policies, no versioning for inline policies, any version except the default can be deleted, and rollback is done by setting the previous version as the default.

Quotes state an account in the Principal element delegates authority to the account, an administrator there must grant access to an IAM user or role, and the account ARN does not limit permissions to the root user.
Quote states the Principal element cannot be used in an identity-based policy and the principal is implicitly the identity where the policy is attached.
Claim repeats the quoted Principal bullet of the JSON policy document structure word for word.
Quote states a user group cannot be a principal in a policy because groups relate to permissions, not authentication.

Quote states service roles must include a trust policy defining which principals can assume the role, in some cases you must specify the service principal, and the service principal cannot be Service: *.

Quote states that for resource-based policies a wildcard with Allow grants access to all users including anonymous users, and principals in other accounts also need identity-based permissions in their account.

Well-Architected quote states IAM users and roles have no permissions by default and the root user has full access and should be used only for tasks that require root access; the IAM FAQ quote states access is denied by default unless a policy explicitly grants it.

Quote states AWS RAM shares resources across accounts, OUs or an entire organization without writing individual resource-based policies for each shared resource.
Claim repeats the quoted sentence from RCP effects on permissions.

Claim says an RCP limits every principal, but the very next sentence of the quoted bullet makes service-linked roles an exception; the quotes support only principals in or outside the organization, including root users, plus the RCP/SCP choice.
FAQ quote states RCPs centrally set the maximum available permissions to your AWS resources, for example restricting access to identities that belong to your organization.

Quotes state an RCP never grants permissions and specifies maximum available permissions for resources, and that RCPs do not affect management account resources and only affect member account resources.
Quote in the RCP bullet states they have no effect on resources in the management account.
Claim repeats the quoted sentence under Resources and entities not restricted by RCPs.

The first quote supports the subset of services, but the second quote only says you cannot change or manage the permissions of AWS managed keys; the sentence that RCPs do not apply to AWS managed KMS keys is in the context, not in any quote.

Quote supports the examples, defining who has access, and using resource-based policies to grant direct cross-account access; it does not say they are 'the way' (exclusivity) nor mention 'without a role'.
Two quotes state resource-based policies are inline only and there are no managed resource-based policies.
